sentences.zh: 梁士彥

translations.literal: Liang Shiyan
translations.idiomatic: Liang Shiyan

sentences.zh: 梁士彥字相如，安定烏氏人也．少任俠，好讀兵書，頗涉經史．周武帝將平東夏，聞其勇決，自扶風郡守除為九曲鎮將，進位上開府，封建威縣公，齊人甚憚之．後以熊州刺史從武帝拔晉州，進位大將軍，除晉州刺史．及帝還後，齊後主親攻圍之，樓堞皆盡，短兵相接．士彥慷慨自若，謂將士曰：「死在今日，吾為爾先！

translations.literal: Liang Shiyan, styled Xiangru, was a native of Wushi in Anding. In youth he was a knight-errant, fond of reading military books and well versed in the classics and histories. When Emperor Wu of Zhou was about to pacify eastern Xia, hearing of his courage and resolution, he was promoted from Administrator of Fufeng to General of Jiuqu Fort, advanced to Upper Opening Grandee, enfeoffed as Duke of Jianwei County, and the Qi people greatly feared him. Later, as Governor of Xiongzhou he followed the Emperor in taking Jinzhou, was promoted to Grand General, and appointed Governor of Jinzhou. After the Emperor returned, the Later Qi ruler personally came to besiege it; the towers and battlements were all destroyed, and they fought at close quarters. Shiyan was generous and calm, and said to his officers and men: "To die is today; I will go before you!
translations.idiomatic: Liang Shiyan, courtesy name Xiangru, came from Wushi in Anding. As a young man he lived by the sword, loved military treatises, and had read widely in the classics and histories. When Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou was preparing to conquer the eastern Qi territories, he heard of Shiyan's bold decisiveness, promoted him from prefect of Fufeng to general of Jiuqu Fort, raised him to Upper Opening Grandee, and enfeoffed him as Duke of Jianwei—so greatly did the Qi fear him. Later, serving as governor of Xiongzhou, he followed the emperor in capturing Jinzhou, was made grand general, and appointed governor of Jin. After the Zhou army withdrew, the Later Qi ruler came in person to besiege the city; every tower and parapet was smashed, and the fighting came to hand-to-hand range. Shiyan remained composed and open-handed, and told his troops: "If we die, we die today—and I will lead you!"

sentences.zh: 」於是勇烈齊奮，呼聲動地，無不一當百．齊師少劔，乃令妻妾及軍人子女，畫夜修城，三日而就．武帝六軍亦至，齊師圍解．士彥見帝，持帝鬚泣，帝亦為之流涕．時帝欲班師，士彥叩馬諫．帝從之，執其手曰：「朕有晉州，為平齊之基，宜善守之．」及齊平，封郕國公，位上柱國、[一]雍州主簿．宣帝即位，除徐州總管．與烏丸軌禽陳將吳明徹、裴忌於呂梁，略定淮南地．

translations.literal: " Thereupon the fierce and valiant leapt forward together; their shouts shook the earth, and not one failed to match a hundred. The Qi army was somewhat reduced. He then ordered wives, concubines, and the women of the army to repair the walls day and night, and in three days it was done. The Emperor's six armies also arrived, and the Qi siege was lifted. Shiyan saw the Emperor, seized his beard and wept, and the Emperor wept for him as well. At that time the Emperor wished to withdraw the army; Shiyan knelt by the horse and remonstrated. The Emperor followed his advice, took his hand, and said: "In having Jinzhou I have the foundation for pacifying Qi; you should guard it well." When Qi was pacified, he was enfeoffed as Duke of the State of Xing, appointed Senior Pillar of State, and [1] Chief Clerk of Yong Province. When Emperor Xuan took the throne, he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Xuzhou. With the Wuhuan Gui he captured the Chen generals Wu Mingche and Pei Ji at Lüliang and largely settled the Huainan region.
translations.idiomatic: " At once the bravest surged forward; their battle cry shook the ground, and each man fought as if he were a hundred. The Qi line wavered. Shiyan then set wives, concubines, and camp followers to repair the walls by day and night, and within three days the defenses stood again. The emperor's main forces arrived and the siege was broken. When Shiyan met the emperor he clutched his beard and wept, and the emperor wept with him. The emperor then meant to withdraw; Shiyan knelt at his horse and pleaded against it. The emperor took his counsel, clasped his hand, and said: "Jinzhou is the base from which Qi will be conquered—guard it well." After the fall of Qi he was made Duke of Xing, senior pillar of state, and [1] chief clerk of Yong province. Under Emperor Xuan he became commander-in-chief of Xuzhou; with the Wuhuan general Gui he took the Chen commanders Wu Mingche and Pei Ji at Lüliang and secured much of Huainan.

sentences.zh: 隋文帝作相，轉亳州總管．尉遲迥反，為行軍總管，及韋孝寬擊之，[二]令家僮梁默等為前鋒，士彥繼之，所當皆破．及迥平，除相州刺史．深見忌，徵還京師．閑居無事，恃功懷怨，與宇文忻、劉昉等謀反．將率僮僕候上享廟之際以發機．復欲於蒲州起事，略取河北，捉黎陽關，塞河陽路，劫調布為牟甲，募盜賊為戰士．其甥裴通知而奏之．帝未發其事，授晉州刺史，欲觀其志．士彥欣然謂昉等曰：「天也！

translations.literal: When Emperor Wen of Sui became Chancellor, he was transferred to Commander-in-Chief of Bozhou. When Yuchi Jiong rebelled, he served as campaign commander; with Wei Xiaokuan he attacked him, [2] appointing his household retainers Liang Mo and others as vanguard while Shiyan followed; wherever they met the enemy they broke them. When Jiong was pacified, he was appointed Governor of Xiangzhou. Deeply regarded with suspicion, he was summoned back to the capital. Idle and with nothing to do, relying on his merit he harbored resentment, and with Yuwen Xin, Liu Fang, and others plotted rebellion. He was to lead his servants and wait for the occasion when the emperor went to enjoy the temple sacrifice to set the plot in motion. He also wished to rise at Puzhou, seize Hebei, take Liyang Pass, block the Heyang road, seize tribute cloth for armor, and recruit bandits as warriors. His nephew Pei Tong learned of it and reported it. The Emperor had not yet revealed the matter, but appointed him Governor of Jinzhou, wishing to observe his intentions. Shiyan said gladly to Fang and the others: "Heaven!" He also requested the Yitong Xue Mo'er as chief clerk, and the Emperor consented.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen of Sui was still regent, Shiyan was made commander-in-chief of Bozhou. During Yuchi Jiong's rebellion he served as a campaign commander under Wei Xiaokuan; [2] he set his household retainer Liang Mo and others in the van and followed with the main body, breaking every force they met. After Jiong's defeat he was made governor of Xiangzhou. The court deeply distrusted him and recalled him to the capital. With nothing to do he brooded on his services and grievances and joined Yuwen Xin, Liu Fang, and others in a plot. He would strike when the emperor went to sacrifice at the ancestral temple, and also planned to raise troops at Puzhou, seize Hebei, hold Liyang Pass, cut the Heyang route, take levy cloth for armor, and enlist bandits as soldiers. His nephew Pei Tong discovered the plot and reported it. The emperor kept his own counsel, appointed him governor of Jinzhou, and watched what he would do. Shiyan exulted to Fang and the rest: "Heaven is with us!" He also asked for the yitong Xue Mo'er as chief clerk, and the emperor granted it.

sentences.zh: 」又請儀同薛摩兒為長史，帝從之．後與公卿朝謁，帝令執士彥、忻、昉等於行間，詰之狀，猶不伏，捕薛摩兒至對之．摩兒具論始末云：「第二子剛垂泣苦諫，第三子叔諧曰：『作猛獸須成斑．』」士彥失色，顧曰：「汝殺我！

translations.literal: Later, when he attended court with the nobles, the Emperor had Shiyan, Xin, Fang, and the others seized in the ranks and questioned about the facts; they still would not confess. Xue Mo'er was captured and confronted with them. Mo'er fully set forth the beginning and end, saying: "The second son Gang wept bitterly and remonstrated; the third son Shuhan said: 'To make a fierce beast you must give it stripes.'" Shiyan changed color and turned, saying: "You have killed me!
translations.idiomatic: Later, at a court audience with the nobles, the emperor had Shiyan, Xin, Fang, and the others seized in the ranks and questioned; they still would not confess. Xue Mo'er was brought in to testify against them. Mo'er laid out the whole affair: "The second son Gang wept and begged him to stop; the third son Shuhan said, 'If you mean to be a tiger, you must earn your stripes.'" Shiyan went pale and cried to his son: "You have killed me!

sentences.zh: 」於是伏誅，時年七十二．有子五人．

translations.literal: " Thereupon he was executed by beheading, aged seventy-two. He had five sons.
translations.idiomatic: " He was then beheaded, at the age of seventy-two. He left five sons.

sentences.zh: 操字孟德，位上開府、義鄉縣公，早卒．

translations.literal: Cao, styled Mengde, held the rank of Upper Opening Grandee and Duke of Yixiang County; he died young.
translations.idiomatic: Cao, courtesy name Mengde, held the rank of upper opening grandee and duke of Yixiang county; he died young.

sentences.zh: 梁剛、梁叔諧

translations.literal: Liang Gang and Liang Shuhan
translations.idiomatic: Liang Gang and Liang Shuhan

sentences.zh: 剛字永固，位大將軍、通政縣公、涇州刺史．以諫公獲免，徙瓜州．叔諧坐士彥誅．

translations.literal: Gang, styled Yonggu, held the rank of Grand General, Duke of Tongzheng County, and Governor of Jingzhou. For remonstrating with his father he was spared execution and banished to Guazhou. Shuhan was executed along with Shiyan.
translations.idiomatic: Gang, courtesy name Yonggu, was grand general, duke of Tongzheng county, and governor of Jingzhou. Because he had remonstrated with his father he was spared and exiled to Guazhou. Shuhan died with Shiyan in the purge.

sentences.zh: 梁默者，士彥之蒼頭也，驍武絕人．士彥每從征伐，常與默陷陣．仕周，位開府．開皇末，以行軍總管從楊素征突厥，進位大將軍．又從平楊諒，授柱國．大業五年，從煬帝征吐谷渾，力戰死之．贈光祿大夫．

translations.literal: Liang Mo was Shiyan's personal slave, surpassing all in martial valor. Whenever Shiyan followed campaigns, Mo often broke the enemy lines with him. In Zhou he reached the rank of Opening Grandee. At the end of the Kaihuang era, as campaign commander he followed Yang Su against the Turks and was promoted to Grand General. He also followed in pacifying Yang Liang and was appointed Pillar of State. In the fifth year of Daye he followed Emperor Yang on the campaign against Tuyuhun and died fighting fiercely. He was posthumously awarded Grand Master for Splendid Happiness.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Mo had been Shiyan's personal slave and was a warrior without peer. In every campaign Mo charged the line beside him. Under the Zhou he reached opening grandee. At the end of Kaihuang he served as campaign commander under Yang Su against the Turks and was made grand general; he helped suppress Yang Liang and was named a pillar of state. In Daye 5 he followed Emperor Yang against Tuyuhun and fell in fierce fighting. He was posthumously made grand master for splendid happiness.

sentences.zh: 元諧，河南洛陽人也．家世貴盛．諧性豪俠，有氣調．少與隋文帝同受業於國子，甚相友愛．後以軍功，累遷大將軍．及帝為相，引致左右．諧謂帝曰：「公無黨，譬如水間一堵牆，大危矣．公其勉之！

translations.literal: Yuan Xie was a native of Luoyang in Henan. His family had been illustrious for generations. Xie was bold and chivalrous, with spirit and mettle. In youth he studied with Emperor Wen at the Imperial Academy and they were very friendly. Later, through military merit he was repeatedly promoted to Grand General. When the Emperor became Chancellor, he was brought to his side. Xie said to the Emperor: "Your Grace has no faction—as though a single wall stood in midstream; it is most perilous. Your Grace should exert yourself!
translations.idiomatic: Yuan Xie came from Luoyang in Henan. His clan had been eminent for generations. He was high-spirited and chivalrous, with force of character. In youth he had studied at the Imperial Academy alongside the future Emperor Wen and they were close friends. Military service raised him repeatedly to grand general. When Wen became regent, Xie was brought to his inner circle. Xie told him: "You stand alone—like a single wall in midstream. That is terribly dangerous. Press on while you can!

sentences.zh: 」及帝受禪，顧諧笑曰：「水間牆竟何如也？

translations.literal: " When the Emperor received the abdication, he looked at Xie and smiled, saying: "How about that wall in midstream?
translations.idiomatic: " When Wen took the throne he turned to Xie and smiled: "Well—how stands that wall in midstream now?

sentences.zh: 」進位上大將軍，封樂安郡公．奉詔參修律令．

translations.literal: " He was promoted to Senior Grand General and enfeoffed as Duke of Le'an Commandery. By imperial order he took part in compiling laws and statutes.
translations.idiomatic: " He was promoted to senior grand general and enfeoffed as duke of Le'an commandery, and by imperial order helped revise the penal code.

sentences.zh: 時吐谷渾將定城王鐘利旁率騎度河，[三]連結党項．諧率兵出鄯州，[四]趣青海，邀其歸路．相遇於豐利山，諧擊走之，又破其太子可博汗．其名王十七人、公侯十三人，各率其所部來降．詔授上柱國，別封一子縣公．諧拜寧州刺史，頗有威惠．然性剛愎，好排詆，不能取媚於左右．嘗言於上曰：「臣一心事主，不曲取人意．」上曰：「宜終此言．」後以公事免．

translations.literal: At that time the Tuyuhun general Dingcheng Wang Zhonglipang led cavalry across the river, [3] linking with the Qiang tribes. Xie led troops out of Shanzhou, [4] marched toward Qinghai, and blocked their line of retreat. They met at Fengli Mountain; Xie attacked and drove them off, and also defeated their crown prince Kebohan. Seventeen lesser kings and thirteen dukes and marquises each led their followers to surrender. By edict he was appointed Senior Pillar of State, and one son was separately enfeoffed as Duke of a county. Xie was appointed Governor of Ningzhou and had considerable prestige and kindness. Yet he was stubborn and willful, fond of slandering others, and could not please those about the throne. He once said to the Emperor: "Your servant serves the ruler with one heart and does not bend to others' wishes." The Emperor said: "You should keep to these words to the end." Later he was dismissed for a public matter.
translations.idiomatic: At that time the Tuyuhun general Zhonglipang of Dingcheng led cavalry across the Yellow River [3] and joined forces with Qiang tribes. Xie marched from Shanzhou [4] toward Qinghai to cut their retreat. At Fengli Mountain he routed them and also defeated the crown prince Kebohan. Seventeen lesser kings and thirteen dukes and marquises came in with their people. He was made senior pillar of state; one son received a separate county dukedom. As governor of Ningzhou he won real respect and goodwill. Yet he was proud and blunt, quick to denigrate others, and could not court the men around the throne. He once told the emperor: "I serve you with a single heart and will not trim my words to please anyone." The emperor replied: "Hold to that always." Later he was removed over a public matter.

sentences.zh: 時上柱國王誼有功於國，與諧俱無位任，每相往來．胡僧告諧、誼謀反，帝按其事，無狀，慰諭釋之．未幾，誼誅，諧漸被疏忌．然以龍潛之舊，每預朝請，恩禮無虧．及平陳，百僚大宴，諧進曰：「陛下威德遠被，臣前請突厥可汗為候正，陳叔寶為令史，今可用臣言．」帝曰：「朕平陳國，本以除逆，非欲誇誕．公之所奏，殊非朕心．突厥不知山川，何能警候？

translations.literal: At that time Senior Pillar of State Wang Yi had merit for the state; he and Xie alike had no office, and they often visited each other. A Buddhist monk reported that Xie and Yi were plotting rebellion; the Emperor investigated the matter and found no evidence, and comforted and released them. Before long Yi was executed, and Xie was gradually regarded with cold suspicion. Yet because of their old ties from before he rose to power, he still attended court audiences, and favor and ritual were not diminished. When Chen was pacified, the hundred officials held a great feast; Xie advanced and said: "Your Majesty's prestige and virtue reach far; your servant formerly asked that the Turkic khan be made lookout and Chen Shubao be made clerk—now your servant's words may be used." The Emperor said: "In pacifying the Chen state I meant to remove rebels, not to boast. What you present is quite contrary to my mind. How could the Turks, not knowing mountains and rivers, serve as sentries?
translations.idiomatic: Senior pillar Wang Yi had served the state well; he and Xie were both out of office and often met. A monk accused them of treason; the emperor investigated, found nothing, and reassured them. Soon Yi was executed, and Xie fell under growing suspicion. Still, because of their bond from before Wen took power, he continued to attend court without loss of ceremony. At the feast celebrating the conquest of Chen, Xie rose and said: "Your prestige reaches far; I once proposed making the Turkic khan your lookout and Chen Shubao your clerk—now those measures may be adopted." The emperor answered: "I conquered Chen to remove rebels, not to play the braggart. Your suggestion is nothing I want. How could Turks who do not know our mountains and rivers keep watch for us?

sentences.zh: 叔寶昏醉，寧堪驅使？

translations.literal: Shubao is muddled and drunk—how could he be driven to service?
translations.idiomatic: And Shubao is a sodden fool—fit to be ordered about?

sentences.zh: 」諧默然而退．

translations.literal: " Xie fell silent and withdrew.
translations.idiomatic: " Xie said nothing more and withdrew.

sentences.zh: 後數歲，有人告諧與從父弟上開府滂、臨澤侯田鸞、上儀同祁緒等謀反．帝令按其事．有司奏：「諧謀令祁緒勒党項兵，即斷巴蜀．時廣平王雄、左僕射高熲二人用事，諧欲譖去之，云：『左執法星動已四年矣，狀一奏，高熲必死．』又言：『太白犯月，光芒相照，主殺大臣，雄必當之．』諧與滂嘗同謁帝，私謂滂曰：『我是主人，殿上者賊也．』因令滂望氣，滂曰：『彼雲似蹲狗走鹿，不如我輩有福德雲．』」帝大怒，諧、滂、鸞、緒並伏誅，籍沒其家．

translations.literal: Several years later someone reported that Xie, with his paternal cousin Upper Opening Grandee Pang, Linze Marquis Tian Luan, Upper Yitong Qi Xu, and others were plotting rebellion. The Emperor ordered an investigation. The officials reported: "Xie plotted to have Qi Xu lead Qiang troops at once and cut off Bashu. At that time Prince of Guangling Xiong and Left Vice Director Gao Feng were in power; Xie wished to slander and remove them, saying: 'The Left Law star has moved for four years already; with one memorial Feng must die.' He also said: 'The White Planet invades the moon, their rays shining on each other; the ruler will kill great ministers, and Xiong must be struck.' Xie and Pang once attended the Emperor together; Xie privately said to Pang: 'I am the master; the one on the throne is the thief.' He then had Pang observe the omens; Pang said: 'Their clouds are like crouching dogs and running deer—nothing like our clouds of fortune.'" The Emperor was greatly enraged; Xie, Pang, Luan, and Xu were all executed by beheading, and their households were confiscated.
translations.idiomatic: Some years later Xie was denounced for plotting with his cousin, upper opening grandee Pang, Marquis of Linze Tian Luan, upper yitong Qi Xu, and others. The emperor ordered an inquiry. The court reported that Xie meant Qi Xu to raise Qiang troops and sever Bashu; that when Prince Xiong of Guangling and the vice director Gao Feng held power, Xie had plotted to destroy them, saying the Left Law star had moved four years—one memorial and Feng would die; that the white planet was crossing the moon, a sign the ruler would kill great ministers and Xiong would fall; and that attending court with Pang he had whispered, "I am the true master; the man on the throne is the thief," then bade Pang read the sky—whereupon Pang said, "Their clouds are crouching dogs and running deer; ours are clouds of fortune." The emperor was furious. Xie, Pang, Luan, and Xu were beheaded and their families attainted.

sentences.zh: 虞慶則

translations.literal: Yu Qingze
translations.idiomatic: Yu Qingze

sentences.zh: 虞慶則，京兆櫟陽人也，本姓魚．其先仕赫連氏，遂家靈武，世為北邊豪傑．父祥，周靈武太守．

translations.literal: Yu Qingze was a native of Liyang in Jingzhao; his original surname was Yu. His ancestors had served the Helian clan and settled at Lingwu, for generations the great families of the northern frontier. His father Xiang was Zhou Administrator of Lingwu.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Qingze came from Liyang in Jingzhao; his family name had been Yu. His forebears had served the Xiongnu Helian house and settled at Lingwu, where for generations they were magnates of the northern marches. His father Xiang was Zhou prefect of Lingwu.

sentences.zh: 慶則幼雄毅，性俶儻，身長八尺，有膽智，善鮮卑語，身被重鎧，帶兩鞬，左右馳射，本州豪俠皆敬憚之．初以射獵為事，中更折節讀書，常慕傅介子、班仲升之為人．仕周，為中外府外兵參軍事，襲爵沁源縣公．越王盛討平稽胡，將班師，內史下大夫高熲與盛謀，須文武幹略者鎮遏之，表請慶則，於是拜石州總管．甚有威惠，稽胡慕義歸者八千餘戶．

translations.literal: Qingze in youth was fierce and resolute, free and unconventional in character, eight feet tall, with courage and wisdom, skilled in Xianbei speech, wearing heavy armor himself, with two quivers at his belt, shooting left and right while riding; the bold spirits of his district all respected and feared him. At first he made his living by hunting; later he changed his ways and read books, often admiring the deeds of Fu Jiezi and Ban Chao. In Zhou he served as Outer Troops Attendant of the Office for All Within and Without, and inherited the title Duke of Qinyuan County. When Prince Sheng of Yue attacked and pacified the Jiehu, as the army was about to withdraw, the Palace Scribe Gao Feng and Sheng plotted that a man of civil and military capacity was needed to hold them down; they memorialized for Qingze, and he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Shizhou. He had great prestige and kindness; more than eight thousand households of Jiehu submitted out of admiration.
translations.idiomatic: In youth Qingze was bold and unyielding, tall and unconventional—eight feet in stature, brave and clever, fluent in Xianbei, able to wear full mail and ride with twin quivers, shooting to either hand. Local heroes feared and honored him. He began as a hunter, then turned to books and modeled himself on Fu Jiezi and Ban Chao. Under the Zhou he was outer-troops attendant in the combined bureau and inherited the dukedom of Qinyuan. When Prince Sheng of Yue crushed the Jiehu and was withdrawing, Gao Feng urged that only a man of both civil and military gifts could hold the region; Qingze was named commander-in-chief of Shizhou. He ruled with authority and kindness, and more than eight thousand Jiehu households submitted to him.

sentences.zh: 開皇元年，歷位內史監、吏部尚書、京兆尹，封彭城郡公，營新都總監．二年，突厥入寇，慶則為元帥討之．部分失所，士卒多寒凍，墮指者千餘人．偏將達奚長儒率騎兵二千人別道邀賊，為虜所圍，慶則按營不救．由是長儒孤軍獨戰，死者十八九．上弗之責也．尋遷尚書右僕射．

translations.literal: In the first year of Kaihuang he successively held the posts of Palace Scribe Supervisor, Minister of Personnel, and Metropolitan Governor of Jingzhao, was enfeoffed as Duke of Pengcheng Commandery, and was Director-General for building the new capital. In the second year the Turks invaded; Qingze served as commander-in-chief to attack them. The disposition of forces was faulty, many soldiers suffered cold and frost, and more than a thousand lost fingers to freezing. The subordinate general Daxi Changru with two thousand horsemen took another road to intercept the enemy and was surrounded by the barbarians; Qingze held camp and did not rescue him. For this Changru fought alone; nine or ten of every ten died. The Emperor did not blame him. Soon he was transferred to Right Vice Director of the Department of State.
translations.idiomatic: In Kaihuang 1 he rose through palace scribe supervisor, minister of personnel, and metropolitan governor of Jingzhao, was made duke of Pengcheng commandery, and oversaw construction of the new capital. In Kaihuang 2, when the Turks raided, he commanded the punitive force. His dispositions failed: troops froze in the field and more than a thousand men lost fingers to the cold. His lieutenant Daxi Changru, with two thousand horse, took a separate road to intercept the enemy and was surrounded; Qingze kept camp and did not relieve him. Changru fought alone until nine in ten of his men were dead. The emperor did not punish him. Soon he was made right vice director of state.

sentences.zh: 後突厥主攝圖將內附，請一重臣充使，詔慶則往．攝圖恃強，慶則責以往事，攝圖不服．其介長孫晟又說諭之，攝圖及弟葉護皆拜受詔，因稱臣朝貢，請永為藩附．初，慶則出使，帝敕曰：「我欲存立突厥，彼送公馬，但取五三疋．」攝圖見慶則，贈馬千疋，又以女妻之．帝以慶則功高，皆無所問．授上柱國，封魯國公，食任城縣千戶，以彭城公迴授第二子義．

translations.literal: Later the Turkic ruler Shetu was about to submit inward and requested a high minister as envoy; by edict Qingze went. Shetu relied on his strength; Qingze reproached him for past conduct, and Shetu would not submit. His attendant Zhangsun Sheng again persuaded him, and Shetu and his younger brother Yehu all bowed to receive the edict, thereafter styled themselves subjects, paid tribute, and asked to remain forever as a border dependency. At first, when Qingze went on the mission, the Emperor instructed him: "I wish to preserve the Turks; if they present horses to you, take only five or six out of ten." Shetu saw Qingze and presented a thousand horses, and also gave him his daughter in marriage. The Emperor, because Qingze's merit was great, made no inquiry into any of it. He was appointed Senior Pillar of State, enfeoffed as Duke of the State of Lu, with a fief of one thousand households at Rencheng County; the Pengcheng dukedom was transferred to his second son Yi.
translations.idiomatic: When the Turkic khan Shetu prepared to submit, he asked for a minister of the first rank as envoy, and Qingze was sent. Shetu blustered; Qingze rebuked him for past offenses and Shetu resisted until Zhangsun Sheng persuaded him. Shetu and his brother Yehu accepted the edict on their knees, styled themselves vassals, sent tribute, and asked to remain a frontier dependency forever. Before Qingze left, the emperor had told him: "I mean to preserve the Turks; if they give you horses, take only five or six in ten." Shetu met him with a gift of a thousand horses and gave him his daughter in marriage. Because Qingze's service was great, the emperor asked no questions. He became senior pillar of state and duke of Lu with a thousand-household fief at Rencheng; the Pengcheng title passed to his second son Yi.

sentences.zh: 平陳後，帝幸晉王第，置酒會戝臣．高熲等奉觴上壽．帝曰：「高熲平江南，虞慶則平突厥，可謂茂功矣．」楊素曰：「皆由至尊威德所被．」慶則曰：「楊素前出兵武牢、硤石，若非至尊威德，亦無剋理．」遂互相長短．御史欲彈之，帝曰：「今日計功為樂，並不須劾．」帝觀戝臣宴射，慶則進曰：「臣蒙賚酒，令盡樂，御史在側，恐醉被彈．」帝賜御史酒，遣之出．慶則奉觴上壽，極歡．帝謂諸公曰：「飲此酒，願我與公等子孫常如今日，世守富貴．」九年，轉為右纫大將軍，尋改為右武候大將軍．

translations.literal: After Chen was pacified the Emperor visited the Prince of Jin's residence, set out wine, and feasted the ministers. Gao Feng and others raised their cups to wish the Emperor long life. The Emperor said: "Gao Feng pacified the Jiangnan, Yu Qingze pacified the Turks—truly abundant merit." Yang Su said: "All is due to Your Majesty's prestige and virtue." Qingze said: "When Yang Su earlier led troops at Wulao and Xiaoshi, if not for Your Majesty's prestige and virtue there would have been no victory." They then vied in praising and blaming each other. The censor wished to impeach them; the Emperor said: "Today we reckon merit for joy; there is no need to impeach." The Emperor watched the ministers feast and shoot; Qingze advanced and said: "Your servant received your gift of wine and was told to enjoy himself fully; with the censor at my side I fear drunken impeachment." The Emperor gave the censor wine and sent him out. Qingze raised his cup to wish the Emperor long life, to the utmost joy. The Emperor said to the nobles: "Drink this wine; may I and you and your sons and grandsons ever be as today, guarding wealth and honor through the generations." In the ninth year he was transferred to Senior General of the Right Guard; soon he was changed to Senior General of the Right Martial Guard.
translations.idiomatic: After the fall of Chen the emperor visited the Prince of Jin, set out wine, and feasted his ministers. Gao Feng and others toasted his long life. The emperor said: "Feng conquered the south; Qingze the Turks—splendid service both." Yang Su said: "All flows from your majesty's virtue." Qingze replied: "When Su took Wulao and Xiaoshi, without your majesty's virtue there would have been no victory." They traded compliments and barbs until the censor moved to impeach them; the emperor said: "Today we count merit for joy—no indictments." Watching the archery feast, Qingze said: "You gave me wine and bade me rejoice fully; with the censor beside me I fear drunken impeachment." The emperor gave the censor wine and sent him away. Qingze toasted the emperor to the height of merriment. The emperor told the assembly: "Drink, and may we and our sons and grandsons keep this day forever." In year 9 he became senior general of the right guard, then of the right martial guard.

sentences.zh: 十七年，嶺南人李世賢據州反，議欲討之．諸將二三請行，皆不許．帝顧謂慶則曰：「位居宰相，爵為上公，國家有賊，遂無行意，何也？

translations.literal: In the seventeenth year the man of Lingnan Li Shixian held the province in rebellion; it was debated that he should be attacked. Two or three generals requested to go, and none was permitted. The Emperor looked at Qingze and said: "You hold the rank of Chancellor, are enfeoffed as Upper Lord, and when the state has bandits you have no mind to go—why?
translations.idiomatic: In year 17 Li Shixian of Lingnan rebelled and held his province. Several generals asked to lead the campaign and were refused. The emperor turned to Qingze: "You stand at the summit of the state, hold the highest noble rank—and when bandits arise you show no will to march. Why?

sentences.zh: 」慶則拜謝恐懼，帝乃遣焉．為桂州道行軍總管，以婦弟趙什柱為隨府長史．什柱與慶則愛妾通，恐事彰，乃宣言：「慶則不欲此行．」帝聞之．先是，朝臣出征，帝皆宴別，禮賜遣之．慶則南討辭帝，帝色不悅，慶則由是怏怏不得志．暨平世賢還，歸桂鎮，[五]觀眺山川形勢，曰：「此誠險固，加以足砕．若守得其人，攻不可拔．」遂使什柱馳詣京奏事，觀帝顏色．什柱至京，因告慶則謀反．帝按驗之，於是伏誅．拜什柱為大將軍．

translations.literal: " Qingze bowed in apology and fear; the Emperor then sent him. He was campaign commander of the Guizhou route; his wife's younger brother Zhao Shizhu was chief clerk of his staff. Shizhu had an affair with Qingze's beloved concubine; fearing exposure, he proclaimed: "Qingze does not wish this campaign." The Emperor heard of it. Before this, when court ministers went on campaign the Emperor always feasted and dismissed them with ritual gifts. When Qingze took leave for the southern expedition and bade the Emperor farewell, the Emperor's countenance was displeased, and Qingze therefore was resentful and could not achieve his aim. When Shixian was pacified he returned and garrisoned Gui, [5] viewing the mountains and rivers and terrain, and said: "This is truly perilous and strong, and in addition the paths are broken. If held by the right man, it cannot be taken by assault." He then sent Shizhu galloping to the capital to report; Shizhu observed the Emperor's expression. When Shizhu reached the capital he reported that Qingze was plotting rebellion. The Emperor investigated and verified it; thereupon Qingze was executed by beheading. Shizhu was appointed Grand General.
translations.idiomatic: " Qingze bowed in terror and was sent as campaign commander of the Guizhou route, with his brother-in-law Zhao Shizhu as chief clerk. Shizhu lay with Qingze's favorite concubine; fearing discovery, he spread word that Qingze did not want the expedition. When Qingze came to take leave, the emperor's face was cold—unlike the farewell feasts given other commanders—and Qingze went south bitter and ill at ease. After defeating Shixian he returned to Gui, surveyed the terrain, and said: "This country is rugged and the roads are shattered; in the right hands it cannot be stormed." He sent Shizhu to court on pretense of business to read the emperor's mood. At the capital Shizhu accused him of treason; the charge was verified and Qingze was beheaded. Shizhu was made grand general.

sentences.zh: 虞孝仁

translations.literal: Yu Xiaoren
translations.idiomatic: Yu Xiaoren

sentences.zh: 慶則子孝仁，幼豪俠任氣，拜儀同，領晉王親信．坐父事除名．煬帝嗣位，以藩邸之舊，授候纫長史，兼領金谷監，監禁苑．有巧思，頗稱旨．大業九年，伐遼，遷都水丞，充使監運，頗有功．然性奢華，以駱駝負函盛水養魚而自給．後或告其為不軌，遂見誅．

translations.literal: Qingze's son Xiaoren in youth was bold and chivalrous and free-spirited; he was appointed Yitong and led the Prince of Jin's personal guard. Because of his father's affair his name was struck from the rolls. When Emperor Yang succeeded, because of old ties from the princely residence he was appointed chief of the guard attendants and concurrently overseer of the Golden Valley Park, supervising the forbidden park. He had clever ideas and was much praised. In the ninth year of Daye, on the Liaodong campaign, he was transferred to Vice Director of Waterways, served as commissioner supervising transport, and had considerable merit. Yet he was extravagant, using camels to carry boxes filled with water to keep fish for his own table. Later someone reported that he was acting improperly, and he was executed.
translations.idiomatic: Qingze's son Xiaoren was a swaggering youth, made yitong and put in charge of the Prince of Jin's household guard. He was struck from the rolls when his father fell. Emperor Yang, remembering their days in the princely mansion, made him chief of the guard attendants and keeper of the Golden Valley Park within the imperial preserve. His ingenuity pleased the court. In Daye 9, on the Liaodong campaign, he became vice director of waterways and transport commissioner with real credit—but he lived lavishly, using camels to carry tanks of water so he could keep fish for his table. Denounced for misconduct, he was executed.

sentences.zh: 元冑，河南洛陽人，魏昭成帝之六代孫也．祖順，魏濮陽王．父雄，武陵王．

translations.literal: Yuan Zhou was a man of Luoyang in Henan, the sixth-generation descendant of Emperor Zhaocheng of Wei. His grandfather Shun was Prince of Puyang of Wei. His father Xiong was Prince of Wuling.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan Zhou came from Luoyang in Henan, sixth-generation descendant of Emperor Zhaocheng of Northern Wei. His grandfather Shun had been Prince of Puyang; his father Xiong, Prince of Wuling.

sentences.zh: 冑少英果，多武藝，美鬚眉，有不可犯之色．周齊王憲見而壯之，引致左右，數從征伐．官至大將軍．隋文帝初被召入，將受顧託，先呼冑，次命陶澄，並委以腹心，恒宿臥內．及為丞相，每典軍在禁中，又引弟威俱入侍纫．

translations.literal: Zhou in youth was heroic and resolute, skilled in many martial arts, with a fine beard and eyebrows and a forbidding countenance. Prince Xian of Qi of Zhou saw him and admired his strength, brought him to his side, and he often followed campaigns. He reached the rank of Grand General. When Emperor Wen of Sui was first summoned to enter [the capital], about to receive the dying charge, he first called Zhou, then ordered Tao Cheng, and entrusted them both with his inmost heart, always lodging them within to sleep. When he became Chancellor, he always commanded the army within the forbidden precinct, and also brought his younger brother Wei to attend within the guard.
translations.idiomatic: As a youth Zhou was bold and accomplished in arms, handsome and severe of face. Prince Xian of Qi took him into his household and often led him on campaign until he became grand general. When the future Emperor Wen was first summoned to the capital to receive the dying regent's charge, he called Zhou first, then Tao Cheng, and gave both men his deepest trust, keeping them to sleep within his quarters. As regent he kept Zhou commanding troops inside the palace and brought his younger brother Wei into the inner guard as well.

sentences.zh: 周趙王招謀害帝，帝不之知，乃將酒肴詣其宅．趙王引帝入寢室，左右不得從，唯楊弘與冑兄弟坐於戶側．趙王令其二子進瓜，因將刺帝．及酒酣，趙王欲生變，以佩刀子刺瓜，連啗帝，將為不利．冑進曰：「相府有事，不可久留．」趙王呵之曰：「我與丞相言，汝何為者！

translations.literal: Prince Zhao of Zhou plotted to harm the Emperor; the Emperor did not know it, and went with wine and food to his residence. Prince Zhao led the Emperor into the inner chamber; those at his side could not follow—only Yang Hong and the Zhou brothers sat by the door. Prince Zhao ordered his two sons to present melons; he then intended to stab the Emperor. When the wine was deep, Prince Zhao wished to make a sudden move, took his girdle knife to cut the melon, and repeatedly offered it to the Emperor, intending harm. Zhou advanced and said: "There is business at the Chancellor's office; you cannot stay long." Prince Zhao shouted at him: "I am speaking with the Chancellor—what are you doing!
translations.idiomatic: Prince Zhao of Zhou plotted against Wen, who did not suspect it and came to his house with wine and food. Zhao led him into an inner room; attendants could not enter—only Yang Hong and the Zhou brothers sat by the door. Zhao had his sons bring melons, then meant to stab the emperor over the cups. As the drinking deepened he drew his belt knife to cut the melon and pressed piece after piece on his guest. Zhou stepped forward: "There is urgent business at the chancellor's office; you cannot linger." Zhao shouted: "I am speaking with the chancellor—what are you doing here!

sentences.zh: 」叱之使劔．冑瞋目憤氣，扣刀入纫．趙王問其姓名，冑以實對．趙王曰：「汝非昔事齊王者乎？

translations.literal: " He shouted at them to draw swords. Zhou glared with angry spirit, drew his knife, and entered the inner chamber. Prince Zhao asked his name; Zhou told him truthfully. Prince Zhao said: "Were you not once in the service of the Prince of Qi? Truly a brave man!
translations.idiomatic: " He ordered them to bare swords. Zhou glared, drew his blade, and entered the inner room. Zhao asked his name; Zhou gave it. Zhao said: "You once served Prince Xian of Qi, did you not? A true champion!

sentences.zh: 誠壯士也！

translations.literal: Truly a brave man!
translations.idiomatic: A true champion!

sentences.zh: 」因賜之酒，曰：「吾豈有不善之意邪？

translations.literal: " He then gave him wine and said: "How could I have ill intent? Why are you so suspicious and on guard!
translations.idiomatic: " He offered wine and said: "I mean you no harm—why so wary?

sentences.zh: 卿何猜警如是！

translations.literal: Why so suspicious and on guard like this!
translations.idiomatic: Why guard against me like this?

sentences.zh: 」趙王偽吐，將入後閤，冑恐其為變，扶令上座，如此者再三．趙王稱喉乾，命冑就箩取飲，冑不動．會滕王逌後至，帝降階迎之，冑耳語勸帝速去．帝猶不悟，曰：「彼無兵馬，復何能為？

translations.literal: " Prince Zhao pretended to vomit and was about to enter the rear apartments; Zhou feared he would make a change, supported him and made him sit in the upper seat, doing this again and again. Prince Zhao said his throat was dry and ordered Zhou to go to the kitchen for drink; Zhou did not move. When Prince Teng You arrived afterward, the Emperor descended the steps to welcome him; Zhou whispered in his ear urging the Emperor to leave quickly. The Emperor still did not understand and said: "They have no troops—what can they do?
translations.idiomatic: " Zhao pretended to retch and moved toward the rear hall; Zhou, fearing a coup, steadied him and forced him back to the seat again and again. Zhao claimed a dry throat and sent Zhou to the kitchen for drink; Zhou would not go. When Prince Teng You arrived, Wen went down to meet him; Zhou whispered that he must leave at once. Wen still said: "They have no soldiers at hand—what can they do?

sentences.zh: 」冑曰：「兵馬悉他家物，一先下手，大事便去．冑不辭死，死何益邪？

translations.literal: " Zhou said: "Their troops and horses are all household property; whoever strikes first, the great affair is gone. Zhou does not shrink from death, but what good is death?
translations.idiomatic: " Zhou said: "Their guards are household retainers—whoever moves first wins everything. I do not fear death, but of what use is my death alone?

sentences.zh: 」復入坐．冑聞屋後有被甲聲，遽請曰：「相府事殷，公何得如此？

translations.literal: " He entered and sat again. Zhou heard behind the house the sound of donning armor, and urgently requested: "Chancellor's business is pressing—how can you remain thus?
translations.idiomatic: " He sat down again. Hearing armor behind the house, he pressed once more: "The chancellor's business is urgent—how can you stay?

sentences.zh: 」因扶帝下祷，趣而去．趙王將追帝，冑以身蔽戶，王不得出．帝及門，冑自後而至．趙王恨不時發，彈指出血．及誅趙王，賞賜不可勝計．

translations.literal: " He then supported the Emperor down from the hall and hurried away. Prince Zhao was about to pursue the Emperor; Zhou shielded the door with his body and the prince could not get out. When the Emperor reached the gate Zhou followed from behind. Prince Zhao regretted that he had not acted in time and cracked his fingernails until they bled. When Prince Zhao was executed, rewards beyond counting were given.
translations.idiomatic: " He half-carried Wen down the steps and rushed out. Zhao tried to pursue; Zhou blocked the doorway and Zhao could not pass. At the gate Zhou came up behind. Zhao, furious that he had hesitated, cracked his nails to the quick. When Zhao was executed, Zhou's rewards were beyond reckoning.

sentences.zh: 帝受禪，封武陵郡公，拜左纫將軍．尋遷右纫大將軍．帝從容曰：「保護朕躬，成此基業，元冑功也．」歷豫、亳、淅三州刺史．時突厥屢為邊患，朝廷以冑素有威名，拜靈州總管，北夷甚憚焉．徵為右纫大將軍，親顧益隆．嘗正月十五日，帝與近臣登高，時冑下直，馳詔召之．及見，謂曰：「公與外人登高，未若就朕也．」賜宴極歡．晉王廣每致禮焉．房陵王之廢也，冑預其謀．帝正窮東宮事，左纫大將軍元旻苦諫，楊素乃譖之．帝大怒，執旻於仗．冑時當下直，不去，因奏曰：「臣向不下直者，為防元旻耳．」復以此言激怒帝，帝遂誅旻．

translations.literal: When the Emperor received the abdication he was enfeoffed as Duke of Wuling Commandery and appointed General of the Left Guard. Soon he was transferred to General of the Right Guard. The Emperor said calmly: "In protecting my person and accomplishing this foundation, Yuan Zhou has the merit." He successively served as Governors of Yu, Bo, and Xi Prefectures. At that time the Turks repeatedly were a border trouble; the court, because Zhou had long had a famous reputation, appointed him Commander-in-Chief of Lingzhou, and the northern barbarians greatly feared him. He was summoned as General of the Right Guard and personal favor increased yet more. Once on the fifteenth of the first month the Emperor with close ministers ascended high; Zhou was off duty but was summoned by urgent edict. When he appeared, the Emperor said: "You went climbing with outsiders—better to come to me." He was given a feast to the utmost joy. Prince Jin Guang often sent him courtesy. In the deposition of the Prince of Fangling, Zhou took part in the plot. The Emperor was then investigating the Eastern Palace affair; Left Guard General Yuan Min remonstrated bitterly, and Yang Su slandered him. The Emperor was greatly enraged and seized Min at the beating staff. Zhou was then going off duty but did not leave, and memorialized: "Your servant did not go off duty because I was guarding against Yuan Min." With these words too he angered the Emperor, and the Emperor then executed Min.
translations.idiomatic: At Wen's accession Zhou was made duke of Wuling commandery and general of the left guard, soon of the right. The emperor said plainly: "He guarded my person and laid this foundation—Zhou's merit." He governed Yu, Bo, and Xi in turn. Because the Turks harried the frontier and Zhou's name alone awed them, he was made commander-in-chief of Lingzhou. Recalled as right-guard general, he stood higher than ever in favor. On a First Month full-moon night the emperor climbed a height with his intimates; Zhou was off duty but was called by urgent edict. "You went sightseeing with outsiders," the emperor said when he came—"better to climb with me." He feasted him royally. Prince Jin Guang often honored him. Zhou took part in the plot to depose the heir of Fangling. While the emperor was probing the eastern palace, left-guard general Yuan Min protested fiercely; Yang Su slandered him. The emperor seized Min for the rod. Zhou was leaving duty but stayed and said: "I did not leave because I feared for Min." That angered the emperor further, and Min was killed.

sentences.zh: 蜀王秀之得罪，冑坐與交通，除名．煬帝即位，不得調．時慈州刺史上官政坐事徙嶺南，將軍丘和亦以罪廢．冑與和有舊，因數從之遊，酒酣，謂和曰：「上官政誠壯士也，今徙嶺表，得無大事乎？

translations.literal: When Prince Xiu of Shu was guilty, Zhou was punished for communicating with him and his name was struck off. When Emperor Yang took the throne he received no appointment. At that time the Governor of Cizhou Shangguan Zheng was punished and banished to Lingnan, and General Qiu He was also dismissed for a crime. Zhou and He were old friends, and therefore often went about with him; when drunk he said to He: "Shangguan Zheng is truly a brave man; now banished beyond the mountains—will there not be a great affair?
translations.idiomatic: When Prince Xiu of Shu fell, Zhou was punished for dealings with him and struck from the rolls. Under Emperor Yang he received no post. Shangguan Zheng, governor of Cizhou, was banished to Lingnan; General Qiu He was also disgraced. Zhou and He were old friends and often drank together; drunk, Zhou told He: "Zheng is a true fighting man—sent to the far south. Will nothing come of that?

sentences.zh: 」因自拊腹曰：「若是公者，不徒然矣！

translations.literal: He then slapped his own belly and said: "If it were you, sir, it would not be in vain!
translations.idiomatic: " He struck his own belly and added: "And if it were you, sir, the story would not end quietly!

sentences.zh: 」和明日奏之，冑竟坐死．於是徵政為驍騎將軍，拜和代州刺史．

translations.literal: " The next day He memorialized it, and Zhou was executed for it. Thereupon Zheng was summoned as General of the Valiant Cavalry, and He was appointed Governor of Daizhou.
translations.idiomatic: " The next day He reported him to the throne, and Zhou was put to death. Zheng was recalled as general of the valiant cavalry; He was made governor of Daizhou.

sentences.zh: 達奚長孺

translations.literal: Daxi Changru
translations.idiomatic: Daxi Changru

sentences.zh: 達奚長孺字富仁，代人也．祖俟，魏定州刺史．父慶，驃騎大將軍、儀同三司．

translations.literal: Daxi Changru, styled Furen, was a native of Dai. His grandfather Yi was Wei Governor of Dingzhou. His father Qing was Grand General of Agile Cavalry and Yitong of the Third Rank.
translations.idiomatic: Daxi Changru, courtesy name Furen, came from Dai. His grandfather Yi had been Wei governor of Dingzhou; his father Qing, grand general of agile cavalry and yitong of the third rank.

sentences.zh: 後與烏丸軌圍陳將吳明徹於呂梁，陳援軍至，軌令長孺拒之．長孺取車輪數百，繫以大石，沈之清水，連轂相次以待之．船艦礙輪不得進，長孺縱奇兵大破之，獲吳明徹，以功進位大將軍．尋授行軍總管，北巡沙塞，卒與虜遇，大破之．

translations.literal: Later, with the Wuhuan Gui he besieged the Chen general Wu Mingche at Lüliang; Chen relief troops arrived, and Gui ordered Changru to resist them. Changru took several hundred cart wheels, tied great stones to them, and sank them in clear water, linking the hubs in succession to await them. The ships were blocked by the wheels and could not advance; Changru released his elite troops and greatly defeated them, capturing Wu Mingche, and through merit was promoted to Grand General. Soon he was appointed campaign commander, patrolled the desert frontier in the north, and at last met the barbarians and greatly defeated them.
translations.idiomatic: With the Wuhuan general Gui he besieged the Chen commander Wu Mingche at Lüliang. When Chen relief came, Gui ordered Changru to hold them off. Changru sank hundreds of cart wheels weighted with stone in the shallows, hub to hub across the channel. The fleet snagged on the wheels and could not pass; he then threw in his picked troops and routed them, taking Wu Mingche and winning promotion to grand general. Soon he patrolled the northern deserts as campaign commander, met the nomads, and broke them decisively.

sentences.zh: 文帝作相，王謙舉兵於蜀，沙氐楊永安扇動利、興、武、文、沙、龍等六州以應謙，詔長孺擊破之．謙二子自京師逃歸其父，長孺並捕斬之．文帝受禪，進位上大將軍，封蘄郡公．

translations.literal: When Emperor Wen became Chancellor, Wang Qian raised troops in Shu; the Shadi Yang Yong'an stirred the six prefectures of Li, Xing, Wu, Wen, Sha, and Long to respond to Qian; by edict Changru defeated them. Qian's two sons fled from the capital to their father; Changru captured and beheaded them both. When the Emperor received the abdication he was promoted to Senior Grand General and enfeoffed as Duke of Qi Commandery.
translations.idiomatic: When Wen was regent, Wang Qian rebelled in Shu; the Shadi chieftain Yang Yong'an roused six prefectures—Li, Xing, Wu, Wen, Sha, and Long—to join him. Changru crushed them by imperial order. Qian's two sons fled the capital to their father; Changru caught and beheaded both. At Wen's accession he became senior grand general and duke of Qi commandery.

sentences.zh: 開皇二年，突厥沙刍略可汗赠弟葉護及藩那可汗寇掠而南，[六]詔以長孺為行軍總管擊之．遇於周槃，红寡不敵，軍中大懼，長孺慷慨，神色愈烈．為虜所衝突，散而復聚，且戰且行，轉岗三日，五兵咸盡，士卒以拳毆之，手皆骨見，殺傷萬計，虜氣稍奪，於是解去．長孺身被五瘡，通中者二，其戰士死者十八九．突厥本欲大掠秦、隴，既逢長孺，兵皆力戰，虜意大沮，明日，於戰處焚屍慟哭而去．文帝下詔褒美，授上柱國，餘勳迴授一子．其戰亡將士，皆贈官三轉，子孫襲之．

translations.literal: In the second year of Kaihuang the Turkic Shabolue Khan and his younger brother Yehu and the dependent khan Fan raided southward, [6] and by edict Changru was campaign commander to attack them. They met at Zhoupan; the troops were few and could not match the enemy; in the army there was great fear, yet Changru was generous and his spirit grew fiercer. He was charged and broken by the barbarians, scattered and gathered again, fighting as he marched for three days; all five weapons were exhausted, and the soldiers beat the enemy with their fists until the bones of their hands showed; those killed and wounded numbered in the tens of thousands, and the barbarians' spirit was somewhat checked, whereupon they withdrew. Changru himself bore five wounds, two through and through; of his warriors nine or ten in ten died. The Turks had intended to plunder greatly in Qin and Long; meeting Changru, all fought with their strength, and the barbarians' intent was greatly depressed. The next day, at the place of battle, they burned the corpses and wailed as they departed. The Emperor issued an edict of praise, appointed him Senior Pillar of State, and transferred the remaining merit to one son. The officers and soldiers who died in battle were all posthumously promoted three ranks, and their sons and grandsons inherited them.
translations.idiomatic: In Kaihuang 2 the khan Shabolue, his brother Yehu, and the dependent khan Fan raided deep south [6]; Changru was sent against them. At Zhoupan he was hopelessly outnumbered and his army was terrified, yet he grew only bolder. The line broke and re-formed; for three days they fought as they marched until every weapon was gone and men beat the enemy with bare fists, bones showing through torn knuckles. Tens of thousands fell on both sides; the Turks' ardor cooled and they drew off. Changru took five wounds, two clean through; nine in ten of his soldiers died. The Turks had meant to strip Qin and Long; meeting him they spent themselves in the fight and went away broken in spirit. Next day they burned their dead on the field and wailed as they left. The emperor praised him in edict, made him senior pillar of state, and ennobled a son with his remaining honors. Every fallen officer was raised three ranks posthumously for his heirs to inherit.

sentences.zh: 歷寧、鄜二州刺史，母憂去職．長孺性至孝，水漿不入口五日，毀悴過禮，殆將滅性，天子嘉歎．起為夏州總管，匈奴憚之，不敢窺塞．以病免．又除襄州總管，轉蘭州．文帝遣涼州總管獨孤羅、原州總管元讣、靈州總管賀若誼等發卒備胡，皆受長孺節度．長孺率红出祁連山北，西至蒲類海，無虜而還．轉荊州總管，帝謂曰：「江陵國之南門，今以委卿，朕無慮也．」卒官．諡曰威．

translations.literal: He successively served as Governor of Ning and Bin Prefectures and left office for his mother's mourning. Changru was extremely filial; for five days he took no water or gruel, and his grief exceeded the rites, nearly destroying his life; the Son of Heaven praised and sighed at it. He was raised as Commander-in-Chief of Xiazhou; the Xiongnu feared him and did not dare peer at the passes. He was dismissed for illness. He was again appointed Commander-in-Chief of Xiangzhou and transferred to Lanzhou. The Emperor sent the Commander-in-Chief of Liangzhou Dugu Luo, the Commander-in-Chief of Yuanzhou Yuan Zha, the Commander-in-Chief of Lingzhou He Ruoyi, and others to raise troops against the Hu, all under Changru's command. Changru led his troops north of the Qilian Mountains, west to Lake Pulei, found no barbarians, and returned. He was transferred to Commander-in-Chief of Jingzhou; the Emperor said to him: "Jiangling is the nation's southern gate; now I entrust it to you—I have no worry." He died in office. His posthumous title was Wei.
translations.idiomatic: He governed Ning and Bin, then left for his mother's mourning. Changru was profoundly filial: five days without food or water, grief beyond the rites, nearly unto death; the emperor marveled and praised him. Recalled, he was commander-in-chief of Xiazhou; the Xiongnu feared him and did not dare test the passes. Illness ended that command. He held Xiangzhou and Lanzhou in turn. The emperor sent Dugu Luo of Liangzhou, Yuan Zha of Yuanzhou, He Ruoyi of Lingzhou, and others to gather troops against the Hu, all under his orders. He marched north of Qilian as far as Lake Pulei, found no enemy, and returned. Made commander-in-chief of Jingzhou, the emperor told him: "Jiangling is the nation's southern gate; I give it to you without anxiety." He died in post. His posthumous name was Wei ("formidable").

sentences.zh: 達奚暠

translations.literal: Daxi Gao
translations.idiomatic: Daxi Gao

sentences.zh: 子暠，大業中，位太僕少卿．

translations.literal: His son Gao, in the Daye era held the post of Vice Director of the Imperial Stud.
translations.idiomatic: His son Gao, in the Daye period, was vice director of the imperial stud.

sentences.zh: 賀婁子幹

translations.literal: Helou Zigan
translations.idiomatic: Helou Zigan

sentences.zh: 賀婁子幹字萬壽，本代人也．隨魏氏南遷，世居關右．祖道成，魏侍中、太子太傅．父景賢，右纫大將軍．

translations.literal: Helou Zigan, styled Wanshou, was originally a man of Dai. Following the Wei when they moved south, his family for generations dwelt in Guanxi. His grandfather Daocheng was Wei Attendant, Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent. His father Jingxian was General of the Right Guard.
translations.idiomatic: Helou Zigan, courtesy name Wanshou, was of Dai origin. When the Wei moved south his family settled in Guanxi for generations. His grandfather Daocheng had been Wei attendant and grand tutor to the heir apparent; his father Jingxian, general of the right guard.

sentences.zh: 子幹少以驍武知名．仕周，累遷少司水，以勤勞封思安縣子．大象中，除秦州刺史，進爵為伯．及尉遲迥為亂，子幹從韋孝寬討之．遇賊圍懷州，子幹與字文述等擊破之．文帝大悅，手書慰勉．其後每戰先登．及破鄴城，與崔弘度逐迥至樓上．進位上開府，封武川縣公，以思安縣伯別封子皎．[七]

translations.literal: Zigan in youth was famous for martial valor. In Zhou he was repeatedly promoted to Vice Director of Water, and through diligence was enfeoffed as Viscount of Si'an County. In the Daxiang era he was appointed Governor of Qinzhou and advanced in rank to Baron. When Yuchi Jiong rebelled, Zigan followed Wei Xiaokuan to attack him. Meeting the rebels besieging Huaizhou, Zigan with Yuwen Shu and others broke them. The Emperor was greatly pleased and personally wrote to comfort and encourage him. Afterward in every battle he led the charge. When Ye city was taken, with Cui Hongdu he pursued Jiong to the tower and killed him. He was promoted to Upper Opening Grandee, enfeoffed as Duke of Wuchuan County, and the Si'an barony was separately enfeoffed on his son Jiao.
translations.idiomatic: In youth Zigan was famed for valor. Under the Zhou he rose to vice director of waterways and, through tireless service, was made viscount of Si'an. In the Daxiang reign he became governor of Qinzhou and a baron. When Yuchi Jiong rebelled he followed Wei Xiaokuan; at the siege of Huaizhou he and Yuwen Shu and others broke the rebel ring. The emperor wrote in his own hand to praise him. In every fight thereafter he led the van. At the fall of Ye he and Cui Hongdu chased Jiong to a tower and killed him. He was made upper opening grandee and duke of Wuchuan; the Si'an barony went to his son Jiao.

sentences.zh: 開皇元年，進爵鉅鹿郡公．其年，吐谷渾寇涼州，子幹以行軍總管從上柱國元諧擊之，功最，優詔褒美，即令子幹鎮涼州．其年，突厥寇蘭州，子幹拒之，至可洛峐山，與賊相遇．賊红甚盛，子幹阻川為營，賊軍不得水數日，人馬甚弊，縱擊，大破之．於是冊授上大將軍，徵授營新都副監，尋拜工部尚書．其年，突厥復犯塞，以行軍總管從竇榮定擊之．子幹別路破賊，文帝嘉之，遣優詔勞勉之．子幹請入朝，詔令馳驛奉見．吐谷渾復寇邊，命子幹討之．入掠其國，二旬而還．

translations.literal: In the first year of Kaihuang he was advanced to Duke of Julu Commandery. That year Tuyuhun raided Liangzhou; Zigan as campaign commander followed Senior Pillar Yuan Xie to attack them and had the highest merit; an excellent edict praised him, and he was immediately ordered to garrison Liangzhou. That year the Turks raided Lanzhou; Zigan resisted them. At Keluoqi Mountain he met the enemy. The enemy troops were very strong; Zigan blocked the stream to make camp, and the enemy army could not obtain water for several days; men and horses were greatly weakened; he then struck and greatly defeated them. Thereupon he was appointed Senior Grand General, summoned as Vice Director-General for building the new capital, and soon appointed Minister of Works. That year the Turks again violated the frontier; as campaign commander he followed Dou Rongding to attack them. Zigan took another road and broke the enemy; the Emperor praised him and sent an excellent edict to comfort and encourage him. Zigan requested to enter court; by edict he was ordered to come by post-horse for audience. Tuyuhun again raided the frontier; he was ordered to attack them. He entered and plundered their country and returned in twenty days.
translations.idiomatic: In Kaihuang 1 he became duke of Julu commandery. That year Tuyuhun raided Liangzhou; as campaign commander under senior pillar Yuan Xie he won top honors and was left to garrison Liangzhou. The Turks then struck Lanzhou; he met them at Keluoqi Mountain. They were numerous; he dammed the stream for his camp and denied them water until men and horses failed—then he attacked and routed them. He was made senior grand general, summoned to help build the new capital, and soon minister of works. Turks raided again; under Dou Rongding he took a separate road, smashed the enemy, and was praised in edict. He asked to attend court and was ordered to come at once by post. Tuyuhun raided once more; he invaded their country and returned within twenty days.

sentences.zh: 文帝以隴西頻被寇掠，甚患之．又彼俗不設村塢，敕子幹勒人為堡，營田積穀，以備不虞．子幹上書曰：「比見屯田之所，獲少費多．但隴右之人，以畜牧為事，若更屯聚，彌不獲安．但使鎮戍連接，烽候相望，人雖散居，必無所慮．」帝從之．

translations.literal: The Emperor, because Longxi was repeatedly ravaged by raids, was greatly troubled by it. Moreover the customs there did not set up village stockades; he ordered Zigan to compel the people to build forts, farm fields, and store grain against emergencies. Zigan memorialized: "Recently in the garrison-farming places, the harvest gained does not repay the expense. But the people of Longyou make animal husbandry their business; if they are further gathered into colonies, they will be even less at ease. Only let the garrison posts connect and beacon fires look upon one another; though the people dwell scattered, there will certainly be no worry." The Emperor followed this.
translations.idiomatic: Longxi had been raided again and again, and the emperor was deeply troubled. The frontier custom did not favor walled villages; he ordered Zigan to force the people into forts, open fields, and store grain against surprise. Zigan wrote: "Garrison farming lately yields less than it costs. Longyou lives by herding; mass resettlement will only unsettle them. Link the posts and let beacon towers see one another; though families stay scattered, no harm need be feared." The emperor agreed.

sentences.zh: 帝以子幹習邊事，授榆關總管，遷雲州刺史，甚為虜所憚．後數年，突厥雍虞閭遣使請降，赠獻羊馬．詔以子幹為行軍總管，出西北道應接之．還，拜雲州總管，以突厥所獻馬百疋、羊千口以賜之，乃下書曰：「自公守北門，風塵不警．突厥所獻，還以賜公．」母憂去職．朝廷以榆關重鎮，尋起視事．卒官．文帝傷惜久之．贈懷、魏等四州刺史，諡曰懷．子善柱嗣．

translations.literal: The Emperor, because Zigan was versed in border affairs, appointed him Commander-in-Chief of Yuguan, transferred him to Governor of Yunzhou, and the barbarians greatly feared him. Several years later the Turkic Yabghu Qaghan sent envoys to request surrender and presented sheep and horses. By edict Zigan was campaign commander and went out by the northwest road to meet them. On his return he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Yunzhou; the horses and sheep presented by the Turks, a hundred head of horses and a thousand sheep, were given to him, and an edict was issued: "Since you guarded the northern gate, the dust of war has not alarmed us. What the Turks presented is returned and given to you." He left office for his mother's mourning. The court regarded Yuguan as a vital stronghold and soon raised him to resume his duties. He died in office. The Emperor mourned and prized him for a long time. He was posthumously awarded Governor of the four prefectures Huai, Wei, and others, with the posthumous title Huai. His son Shanchu inherited.
translations.idiomatic: Knowing the border, the emperor made him commander-in-chief of Yuguan, then governor of Yunzhou, where the nomads feared him. Years later the Turkic yabghu sent envoys to submit with sheep and horses; Zigan went out the northwest road to receive them. Returning, he was again commander-in-chief of Yunzhou; the hundred horses and thousand sheep of the tribute gift were given to him with the words: "Since you held the northern gate, no war-dust has troubled us—take the Turks' offering for yourself." He mourned his mother; Yuguan was too vital to leave empty long, and he was recalled to duty. He died in office; the emperor mourned him long. Posthumously he was made governor of four prefectures including Huai and Wei, with the posthumous name Huai ("cherishing"). His son Shanchu succeeded.

sentences.zh: 賀婁詮

translations.literal: Helou Quan
translations.idiomatic: Helou Quan

sentences.zh: 子幹兄詮，亦有才器．位銀青光祿大夫、鄭純深等三州刺史、北地太守、東安郡公．

translations.literal: Zigan's elder brother Quan also had talent and capacity. He held the rank of Silver-Gleaming Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Governor of the three prefectures Zheng, Chun, and Shen, Administrator of Beidi, and Duke of Dong'an Commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Zigan's elder brother Quan was also a capable man: silver-gleaming grand master for splendid happiness, governor of Zheng, Chun, and Shen, prefect of Beidi, and duke of Dong'an commandery.

sentences.zh: 史萬歲

translations.literal: Shi Wansui
translations.idiomatic: Shi Wansui

sentences.zh: 史萬歲，京兆杜陵人也．父靜，周滄州刺史．

translations.literal: Shi Wansui was a native of Duling in Jingzhao. His father Jing was Zhou Governor of Cangzhou.
translations.idiomatic: Shi Wansui came from Duling in Jingzhao. His father Jing had been Zhou governor of Cangzhou.

sentences.zh: 萬歲少英武，善騎射，驍健若飛．好讀兵書，兼精占候．年十五，逢周、齊戰於芒山，萬歲從父在軍，旗鼓正相望，萬歲令左右趣裝急去．俄而周兵大敗，其父由是奇之．及平齊之役，其父戰沒，萬歲以忠臣子，拜開府儀同三司，襲爵太平縣公．

translations.literal: Wansui in youth was heroic and martial, skilled in riding and shooting, swift and strong as in flight. He loved reading military books and was also skilled in divination and observation of omens. At fifteen, when Zhou and Qi fought at Mangshan, Wansui followed his father in the army; the banners and drums faced each other directly; Wansui ordered those at his side to pack quickly and depart in haste. Before long the Zhou army was greatly defeated; his father therefore marveled at him. In the campaign to pacify Qi his father died in battle; Wansui, as the son of a loyal minister, was appointed Opening Grandee, Yitong of the Third Rank, and inherited the title Duke of Taiping County.
translations.idiomatic: In youth Wansui was bold in arms, a superb horseman and archer, swift as if he could fly. He studied war manuals and read the stars. At fifteen, when Zhou and Qi met at Mangshan, he was with his father in the ranks; as the lines faced each other he ordered his men to pack and move at once. The Zhou army was soon routed, and his father knew him for something extraordinary. In the conquest of Qi his father fell in battle; as a loyalist's son Wansui was made opening grandee, yitong of the third rank, and duke of Taiping county.

sentences.zh: 尉遲迥之亂，萬歲從梁士彥擊之．軍次馮翊，見戝雁飛來，萬歲謂士彥請射行中第三者．射之，應弦而落，三軍莫不悅服．及與迥軍遇，每戰先登．鄴城之陣，官軍稍劔，萬歲乃馳馬奮擊，殺數十人，红亦齊力，官軍復振．迥平，以功拜上大將軍．

translations.literal: In Yuchi Jiong's rebellion Wansui followed Liang Shiyan to attack him. The army halted at Fengyi; he saw battle geese flying and said to Shiyan, asking to shoot the third in the line. He shot, and it fell at the sound of the string; the three armies were all pleased and submitted. When they met Jiong's army, in every battle he led the charge. In the battle array at Ye city the government army was somewhat reduced; Wansui then galloped and struck fiercely, killing several tens of men; the troops also exerted their strength together, and the government army revived. When Jiong was pacified, through merit he was appointed Senior Grand General.
translations.idiomatic: In Yuchi Jiong's rebellion he served under Liang Shiyan. Halting at Fengyi, he saw wild geese in flight and asked leave to shoot the third in line; the bird dropped at the twang and the whole army took heart. In every clash with Jiong he led the charge. At Ye the imperial line faltered; Wansui spurred in, killed dozens of men, and the troops rallied behind him until Jiong was destroyed. He was made senior grand general for his merit.

sentences.zh: 開皇初，大將軍尒朱勣以謀反伏誅，萬歲頗關涉，坐除名，配敦煌為戍卒．其戍主甚驍武，每單騎深入突厥中，輒大剋獲，突厥莫敢當．其人深自矜負，數罵辱萬歲．萬歲患之，自言亦有武用．戍主試令騎射，笑曰：「小人定可．」萬歲因請弓馬，復掠突厥中，大得六畜而歸．戍主始善之，每與同行，輒入突厥數百里，名讋北夷．竇榮定之擊突厥，萬歲詣轅門請自刋．榮定素聞其名，見而大悅．因遣人謂突厥，當各遣一壯士決勝負．突厥許諾，因遣一騎挑戰．榮定遣萬歲出應之，萬歲馳斬其首而還．突厥大驚，遂引軍去．由是拜上儀同，領車騎將軍．平陳之役，以功加上開府．

translations.literal: In the beginning of Kaihuang the Grand General Erzhu Xun was executed for plotting rebellion; Wansui was somewhat implicated, was punished by removal of name, and was assigned to Dunhuang as a garrison soldier. The garrison commander was very martial; each time he rode alone deep into the Turks he always captured greatly, and the Turks did not dare oppose him. That man was deeply proud, and several times reviled and insulted Wansui. Wansui resented this and said he too had martial ability. The garrison commander tested him in riding and shooting and laughed: "The little fellow will do." Wansui therefore requested bow and horse, again raided among the Turks, and returned with great herds of livestock. The garrison commander at first was pleased with him and often went with him; they entered several hundred li into the Turks, and his name awed the northern barbarians. When Dou Rongding attacked the Turks, Wansui went to the camp gate and requested to atone with his head. Rongding had long heard his name and was greatly pleased when he saw him. He therefore sent men to tell the Turks that each side should send one stalwart to decide victory and defeat. The Turks agreed and sent one horseman to challenge. Rongding sent Wansui out to meet him; Wansui galloped and cut off his head and returned. The Turks were greatly alarmed and then led their army away. Thereupon he was appointed Upper Yitong and led the Cavalry General. In the Chen campaign, through merit he was advanced to Upper Opening Grandee.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Kaihuang Grand General Erzhu Xun was executed for treason; Wansui was lightly implicated, struck from the rolls, and sent to Dunhuang as a convict soldier. His garrison chief was a terror who rode alone deep into Turk country and always came back laden with booty. He mocked Wansui until Wansui proved himself in bow and saddle, raided the Turks again, and returned with great herds. The chief took him on raids hundreds of li into the steppe until Wansui's name alone frightened the north. When Dou Rongding campaigned against the Turks, Wansui came to the gate offering his life for service. Rongding knew the name and welcomed him. He proposed single combat; the Turks sent a champion; Wansui rode out and returned with his head. The Turks withdrew in shock. He was made upper yitong and cavalry commander. In the Chen war he won upper opening grandee.

sentences.zh: 及高智慧等作亂江南，以行軍總管從楊素擊之．萬歲自東陽別道而進，踰嶺越海，攻陷溪洞不可勝數．前後七百餘戰，轉岗千里，寂無聲問者十旬，遠近皆以萬歲為沒．萬歲乃置書竹筒中，浮之水．汲者得之，以言於素．大悅，上其事．文帝歎嗟．還，拜左領軍將軍．

translations.literal: When Gao Zhihui and others rebelled in the Jiangnan, as campaign commander he followed Yang Su to attack them. Wansui from Dongyang took a separate road, crossed ranges and seas, and captured streams and caves beyond counting. In more than seven hundred battles before and after, he marched a thousand li in turn; for ten weeks there was silence, no word from him; near and far all thought Wansui was lost. Wansui then placed a letter in a bamboo tube and floated it on the water. One who drew water found it and told Su. Su was greatly pleased and reported it upward. The Emperor sighed in admiration. On his return he was appointed General of the Left Guards.
translations.idiomatic: When Gao Zhihui and others rose in the south he campaigned under Yang Su. From Dongyang he took a separate route over mountains and sea, storming countless ravine strongholds. In more than seven hundred fights he marched a thousand li out of contact; for ten weeks no word came, and men thought him dead. He sealed a report in bamboo, set it on the water, and a drawer's bucket brought it to Su, who reported up in delight. The emperor marveled. On return he was general of the left guard.

sentences.zh: 先是，南寧夷爨翫降，拜昆州刺史，既而復叛．遂以萬歲為行軍總管擊之．入蜻蛉川，經弄凍，次小勃弄、大勃弄，至于南中．賊前後屯據要害，萬歲皆擊破之．行數百里，見諸葛亮紀功碑，銘其背曰：「萬歲後，勝我者過此．」萬歲令左右倒其碑而進．度西二河，[八]入渠濫川，行千餘里，破其三十餘部．諸夷大懼，遣使請降，獻明珠徑寸．於是勒石頌美隋德．萬歲請將爨翫入朝，詔許之．爨翫陰有二心，不欲詣闕，因賂萬歲金寶，萬歲乃捨翫而還．蜀王在益州，知其受賂，遣使將索之．萬歲聞而悉以所得金寶沈之於江，索無所獲．以功進柱國．晉王廣甚欽敬之，待以交友之禮．上知為晉王所善，令萬歲督晉王府軍事．

translations.literal: Earlier the southern barbarian Cuan Wan surrendered and was appointed Governor of Kunzhou, then rebelled again. Thereupon Wansui was campaign commander to attack him. He entered the Qingling River, passed Nongdong, halted at Lesser Nongdong and Greater Nongdong, and reached the southern center. The rebels before and after held strategic points; Wansui all attacked and broke them. Marching several hundred li, he saw Zhuge Liang's monument recording merit; he inscribed on its back: "After ten thousand years, he who surpasses me will pass here." Wansui ordered his attendants to overturn the stele and advance. Crossing the two western rivers, [8] he entered the Quluan River, marched more than a thousand li, and broke more than thirty tribes. The various barbarians were greatly afraid and sent envoys to request surrender, presenting a pearl an inch in diameter. Thereupon he carved stone to praise Sui virtue. Wansui requested to bring Cuan Wan into court; by edict this was permitted. Cuan Wan secretly had two minds and did not wish to come to court; he therefore bribed Wansui with gold and treasures, and Wansui let Wan go and returned. The Prince of Shu was in Yizhou and knew he had accepted bribes; he sent men to seize them. Wansui heard and sank all the gold and treasures he had obtained into the river; nothing could be found. Through merit he was advanced to Pillar of State. Prince Jin Guang greatly respected and honored him, treating him with the ritual of friendship. The Emperor knew he was favored by the Prince of Jin and ordered Wansui to supervise the Prince of Jin's military affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier the Nanning chieftain Cuan Wan had submitted and been made governor of Kunzhou, then rebelled again. Wansui was sent against him. He entered the Qingling, passed Nongdong, and pushed through Lesser and Greater Nongdong into the southern heartland, breaking every strongpoint. After several hundred li he came to Zhuge Liang's victory stele and wrote on the back: "In ten thousand years, whoever surpasses me will pass here," then had it overturned and marched on. Crossing the two western rivers [8] into the Quluan, he went more than a thousand li and shattered thirty-odd tribes. The tribes in terror sent envoys with a pearl an inch across and he carved stone praising Sui virtue. He asked to escort Cuan Wan to court; the edict agreed. Wan bribed him with gold and treasure not to go; Wansui left him and withdrew. Prince Xiu of Shu, knowing the bribe, sent to seize the goods; Wansui sank everything in the river and nothing was found. He was made a pillar of state. Prince Jin Guang honored him as a friend. The emperor, knowing the prince's fondness for him, set Wansui over the prince's military household.

sentences.zh: 明年，爨翫復反．蜀王秀奏萬歲受賂縱賊，致生邊患．上令窮之，事皆驗，罪當死．上數之，萬歲曰：「臣留翫者，恐其州有變，留以鎮撫．臣還至瀘水，詔書方到，由是不將入朝，實不受賂．」上以萬歲心有欺隱，大怒，顧有司曰：「將斬之．」萬歲懼而服罪，頓首請命．左僕射高熲、左纫大將軍元旻等進曰：「史萬歲雄略過人，每行兵用師之處，未嘗不身先士卒，雖古名將未能過也．」上意稍解，於是除名．歲餘，復官爵．尋拜河州刺史，復領行軍總管以備胡．

translations.literal: The next year Cuan Wan rebelled again. Prince Xiu of Shu memorialized that Wansui had accepted bribes and released the bandit, causing border trouble. The Emperor ordered a full investigation; the facts were all verified, and the crime deserved death. The Emperor enumerated his crimes; Wansui said: "Your servant kept Wan because I feared his province would change; I kept him to pacify and hold it. When your servant returned to the Lushui, the edict had just arrived—therefore I did not bring him into court; in truth I did not accept bribes." The Emperor, because Wansui's heart had deceit, was greatly enraged, looked at the officials and said: "Cut off his head." Wansui in fear confessed guilt and knocked his head begging for his life. Left Vice Director Gao Feng, Left Guard General Yuan Min, and others advanced and said: "Shi Wansui's heroic strategy surpasses others; wherever he leads troops and uses the army, he has never failed to go before the soldiers in person—though ancient famous generals could not surpass him." The Emperor's mind was somewhat eased, and thereupon his name was struck off. After more than a year his office and enfeoffment were restored. Soon he was appointed Governor of Hezhou and again campaign commander to guard against the Hu.
translations.idiomatic: The next year Cuan Wan rebelled again. Prince Xiu charged that Wansui had taken bribes, released the rebel, and brought border disaster. Inquiry proved every point; death was due. The emperor listed his crimes; Wansui said: "I left Wan because I feared his province would rise; I meant to pacify it. When I reached the Lushui your edict had only just arrived—that is why I did not bring him in; I took no bribe." The emperor, believing he still lied, raged and ordered his head. Wansui confessed and begged for life. Gao Feng, Yuan Min, and others pleaded: "Wansui's genius in war surpasses all; no ancient name equals a commander who always leads the charge." The emperor relented; his name was struck off. After a year rank and fief returned; soon he was governor of Hezhou and again frontier campaign commander against the Hu.

sentences.zh: 開皇末，突厥達頭可汗犯塞，上令晉王及楊素出靈武道，漢王諒與萬歲出馬邑道．萬歲率柱國張定和、大將軍李藥王、楊義臣等出塞，至大斤山，遇虜．達頭遣使問曰：「隋將為誰？

translations.literal: At the end of Kaihuang the Turkic khan Datou violated the frontier; the Emperor ordered the Prince of Jin and Yang Su to go out by the Lingwu road, Prince of Han Liang and Wansui by the Mayi road. Wansui led Pillars of State Zhang Dinghe, Grand Generals Li Yaowang, Yang Yichen, and others out of the passes; at Mount Dajin they met the barbarians. Datou sent envoys to ask: "Who is the Sui general?
translations.idiomatic: At the end of Kaihuang the khan Datou raided the border. The emperor sent the Prince of Jin and Yang Su by the Lingwu road, the Prince of Han and Wansui by Mayi. Wansui led Zhang Dinghe, Li Yaowang, Yang Yichen, and others beyond the passes to Mount Dajin, where they met the enemy. Datou sent to ask: "Who commands the Sui army?

sentences.zh: 」候騎曰：「史萬歲也．」突厥復曰：「得非敦煌戍卒乎？

translations.literal: The scout said: "Shi Wansui." The Turks again said: "Is he not the Dunhuang garrison soldier?
translations.idiomatic: The scout answered: "Shi Wansui." The Turks asked again: "Not the convict soldier from Dunhuang?

sentences.zh: 」候騎曰：「是也．」達頭聞而引去．萬歲馳追百餘里乃及，擊大破之，逐北入磧數百里，虜遁逃而還．楊素害其功，譖萬歲云：「突厥本降，初不為寇．」遂寢其功．萬歲數抗表陳狀，上未之悟．會上從仁壽宮初還京師，廢皇太子，窮東宮黨與．上問萬歲所在，萬歲實在朝堂，楊素見上方怒，因曰：「萬歲謁東宮矣．」以激怒上．上謂信然，令召萬歲．時所將士卒在朝堂稱垉者數百人，萬歲謂曰：「吾今日為汝極言於上．」及見上，言將士有功，為朝廷所抑，詞氣憤厲，忤上．上大怒，命左右剀殺之．既而追悔不及，因下詔罪狀之．萬歲死之日，天下士庶聞者，識與不識，無不垉惜．

translations.literal: The scout said: "It is he." Datou heard and led his army away. Wansui galloped in pursuit for more than a hundred li before overtaking them, struck and greatly defeated them, pursued north into the desert for several hundred li, and the barbarians fled and escaped and he returned. Yang Su envied his merit and slandered Wansui, saying: "The Turks had originally submitted and were not invaders in the first place," and thus suppressed his merit. Wansui several times submitted memorials stating the facts; the Emperor did not perceive it. When the Emperor returned from Renshou Palace to the capital for the first time and deposed the Crown Prince, he investigated the Eastern Palace faction. The Emperor asked where Wansui was; Wansui was in fact in the court hall. Yang Su saw the Emperor was angry and therefore said: "Wansui has gone to visit the Eastern Palace." to provoke the Emperor. The Emperor believed it true and ordered Wansui summoned. At that time the soldiers he led, several hundred men in the court hall calling for grief, Wansui said to them: "Today I will speak to the utmost for you before the Emperor." When he saw the Emperor he said the officers and soldiers had merit and were suppressed by the court; his words were fierce and he offended the Emperor. The Emperor was greatly enraged and ordered the attendants to hack him to death. Afterward he regretted it and could not recover him; he therefore issued an edict listing his crimes. On the day Wansui died, among gentlemen and commoners throughout the realm, whether they knew him or not, none did not grieve and choke with sorrow.
translations.idiomatic: "It is he." Datou withdrew. Wansui chased more than a hundred li, caught them, and broke them, pursuing into the desert for hundreds of li before turning back. Yang Su, jealous, lied that the Turks had already submitted and were not true invaders, and Wansui's honors were buried. He memorialized again and again; the emperor would not see it. When the emperor returned from Renshou Palace to depose the crown prince and purge the eastern palace faction, he asked where Wansui was—he was in the hall. Su, seeing the emperor's wrath, said Wansui had gone to the heir's palace. Believing it, the emperor summoned him; hundreds of his soldiers in the hall groaned aloud. Wansui told them: "Today I will plead for you to the utmost." Before the emperor he said his men were meritorious and wronged; his tone was fierce and defiant. The emperor ordered him hacked to death, then repented too late and issued a bill of crimes. The day he died, whether men knew him or not, the realm grieved as if choking.

sentences.zh: 萬歲為將，不修營伍，令士卒各隨所安，無警夜之備，虜亦不敢犯．臨陣對敵，應變無方，號為良將．子懷義嗣．

translations.literal: As a general Wansui did not regulate camp formations, ordering the soldiers each to settle where they would, with no night watch against surprise; the barbarians also did not dare violate him. Facing the enemy in battle he responded to change without fixed method and was called a good general. His son Huaiyi inherited.
translations.idiomatic: As a commander he did not fuss over camp layout: each man settled where he pleased, with no formal night watch, yet the nomads did not dare test him. In battle he adapted without set form and was counted a master. His son Huaiyi succeeded.

sentences.zh: 劉方，京兆長安人也．性剛決，有膽氣．仕周，承御上士，以戰功拜上儀同．隋文帝為丞相，方從韋孝寬破尉遲迥於相州，以功加開府，賜爵河陰縣侯．文帝受禪，進爵為公．開皇三年，從纫王爽破突厥於白道，進位大將軍．後歷甘、瓜二州刺史．

translations.literal: Liu Fang was a native of Chang'an in Jingzhao. His nature was firm and decisive, with courage and mettle. In Zhou he was Attendant of the Imperial Carriage, Upper Scholar, and through military merit was appointed Upper Yitong. When Emperor Wen of Sui was Chancellor, Fang followed Wei Xiaokuan in breaking Yuchi Jiong at Xiangzhou; through merit he was advanced to Opening Grandee and enfeoffed as Marquis of Heyin County. When the Emperor received the abdication he was advanced to Duke. In the third year of Kaihuang he followed Prince of Jin Shuang in breaking the Turks at Baidao and was promoted to Grand General. Later he successively served as Governor of Gan and Gua Prefectures.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Fang came from Chang'an in Jingzhao—resolute, brave, and spirited. Under the Zhou he was attendant of the imperial carriage and upper scholar, then upper yitong for military merit. When Wen was regent, Fang followed Wei Xiaokuan in defeating Yuchi Jiong at Xiangzhou, was made opening grandee and marquis of Heyin, and at the accession became a duke. In Kaihuang 3 he followed Prince Shuang of Jin at Baidao against the Turks and was made grand general, later governing Gan and Gua.

sentences.zh: 仁壽中，交州俚人李佛子作亂，據越王故城．左僕射楊素言方有將帥略，於是詔方為交州道行軍總管，統二十七營而進．法令嚴肅，然仁而愛士．長史、度支侍郎敬德亮從軍至尹州，疾甚，不能進，留之州館．分別之際，方哀其危篤，流涕嗚咽，感動行路．論者多之，稱為良將．至都降嶺，遇賊，方遣營主宋纂、何貴、嚴願等破之．進兵臨佛子，先令人諭以禍福，佛子乃降，送於京師．其有桀黠恐為亂者，皆斬之．

translations.literal: In the Renshou era the Liao man of Jiaozhou Li Fozi rebelled and held the old city of the King of Yue. Left Vice Director Yang Su said Fang had the strategy of a commander; thereupon by edict Fang was campaign commander of the Jiaozhou route, commanding twenty-seven camps as he advanced. His laws and orders were strict, yet he was benevolent and loved his soldiers. Chief Clerk and Expenditure Vice Director Jing Deliang followed the army to Yin Prefecture, fell gravely ill, and could not advance; he was left at the prefectural lodge. At the parting Fang grieved at his danger, wept and sobbed, moving those on the road. Many in discussion praised him, calling him a good general. Reaching Dujiang Ridge he met bandits; Fang sent camp commanders Song Zuan, He Gui, Yan Yuan, and others to break them. Advancing his army to Fozi, he first sent men to instruct him in disaster and blessing; Fozi then surrendered and was sent to the capital. Those who were stubborn and feared to make trouble were all beheaded.
